Presidential Ramblings
By Steve Hansen
Welcome back everyone to a new and exciting season. For those of you that have been around for
years, you’ll know that we have a strong tradition
of bringing in world class turners to show us how
they do things. For those newer to the turning fraternity, the sharing of techniques, tips, and tricks, is
part of our wood turning culture. Attending these
day long demos and enrolling in a hands-on class
presented by our guest speakers is a sure way to
elevate your skills and accelerate your enjoyment
of our craft.
“That’s the whole point!” as David Ellsworth has
stated on the magic that is hollow turning through
a small hole. And our first guest speaker of the season, Kevin Jesequel who has studied under David,
will show us how it can be done with simple tools
and a methodical process that makes it far easier
than you might think. Be sure to mark October 25
for his full day demo on that and a few other exciting things.
And the following WEEK, we have an exciting artist,
Yann Morot a teacher from the renowned Escoulen
School
https://www.escoulen.com/?lg=uk
in
France. The French seem to lead the turning world
in new directions, slightly ahead of The Curve so to
speak. Along with Kevin, they are both conducting
classes. Yann will also do a full day Saturday demo
on November 1st.
Great stuff I think! President’s challenge for October is Natural Edge.
Steve

A great woodturner, member of both the Fraser
Valley and Greater Vancouver Woodturners Guilds
for many years, and mentor to many, Bill Olsen,
passed away on September 5.
Bill has turned many bowls, platters, dishes, and
many other pieces at his shop in Surrey. He invited
woodturners of all levels to his shop and tutored
them in the fine arts of our craft. It was Bill who
first introduced me to the guilds after meeting him
at Windsor Plywood in 2000 when I was buying
some glue. Bill has been a great friend ever since
and he will be sorely missed.
Bill's Memorial Service will be held on Oct 25,
2025, at 1:00 pm at the Cloverdale Baptist Church,
18685 64th Ave., Surrey, BC

I Think I’m a Wabi Sabi Kinda Guy
By Ed Pretty
I’m a little laid up right now, so have some time to
contemplate the things around me that I find
“artistic”, really attractive or just plain cool. Most
of it is what I consider “wabi sabi”. I’ve been tossing the idea of writing about wabi sabi in my head
for quite some time but as I contemplate an old
steamer trunk in our office (more about that later),
I am moved to finally put key strokes to screen. I
considered keeping those of you who aren’t familiar with the term “wabi sabi” in suspense by hinting
at various tidbits line after line, but I think I will
forego the drama.
Wabi Sabi is a Japanese aesthetic referring to finding beauty in things imperfect, incomplete or impermanent. Often asymmetry and simplicity are
part of the package. It’s about things that are modest and humble and often things that are unconventional. A dandelion gone to seed is at the same
time exquisite, symmetrical, yet very impermanent. Perhaps the impermanence puts the whole
thing in perspective. So, you see, there is no simple
explanation.
It's good to understand at this point that wabi sabi
refers not to just artistic objects but everything
that surrounds us.
Not long ago, I got a book about Wabi Sabi so that I
could truly understand its meaning. As sometimes
happens, you must be careful what you wish for.
For something that seemingly is all about “Simple”,
it’s unbelievably complex and deep. In seeking the
essence of the thing, I found lots of subjective substance but zero quantitative. In the end I came out
more confused than I went in. I decided that I liked
the fact that it is also something that is easily
“felt”, so that works for me. It brought to mind a
time when I decided I was going to learn the meaning of First Nation abstract symbols representing all
the creatures in their world including themselves. I
came away being able to identify many of them but
also found that one must grow up in the culture to
truly understand the meaning of the interactions
between them all. It's the same with wabi sabi.
But I digress…
As a kid I was surrounded by many things from the
early twentieth century, assembled by my grandparents. They were well-healed and well-travelled,
so some pieces are exquisite art, some are merely
decorative pieces but very attractive, and some are
well-made utilitarian pieces, but with character.
Together, the lot represents many types of skilled
craftspeople and artists. I have always – as are
many people – been attracted by exquisite forms,
beautiful carving and vibrant colours. But many of
the pieces that I recalled and kept close were the
things that had some flaw, asymmetry or patina
that made them unique. That steamer trunk, handbuilt like a tank, has at the same time screws symmetrically aligned, wood joints visible but spot-on
and rugged iron straps that show the blacksmith’s
deftly irregular blows. The dings and scars from
rough handling are evident. The package as a
whole tells a story that was never intended at its
inception but speaks volumes now. Time played a
big role in that.
Interestingly, even though all these pieces that I
find attractive may be somehow flawed, asymmetrical, or “not beautiful” in some way – none are
(Continued on page 5)

September 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page
5
poorly made. Usually, the craftsmanship is beyond
reproach. So, in my opinion, poor craftsmanship
doesn’t give a piece an automatic “wabi sabi” buy
in. Telling a story does, however.
I was first drawn to consciously creating something
with a “wabi sabi” aesthetic when I decided to repair cracks or inclusions in bowl blanks that had
cracked during the drying process (I have plenty). It
is such a shame – neigh, immoral – to toss out a
perfectly good piece of wood that can do the job
but has a flaw. I have made repairs out of necessity
in the past when I repaired a crack after the fact
that seemed attractive at the time, but this was the
first time I set out to create a piece from the outset
with the idea of including the repair as part of the
story. At about the same time I stumbled upon a
video about the Japanese art of Kintsugi, which is
the art of repairing cracked or broken pottery with
lacquers. Kintsugi is a perfect example of the core
meaning of wabi sabi: a perhaps utilitarian piece
that is broken and no longer useful, reborn as a
beautifully restored and revered piece of art. As a
result, I “borrowed” (stole?) the term as the title of
my series of bowls repaired with dovetail patches.
The idea of repairing turned items with dovetail
patches (referred to as “pewa” by Hawaiian turners) is definitely not new to woodturning at large
but is new to my process. Hence, my Kintsugi series.
The very first piece I repaired with dovetails came
to me cracked almost into two pieces. I repaired it
successfully (Whew!) and the owner now displays
it upside down to show off the repair. Thinking
back, this was the inspiration that caused me to
start my Kintsugi series.
So, wabi sabi is new to me, but also not new to me.
While doing my homework I learned some nuanced
things about wabi sabi and have a reasonable understanding of the concept, but it seems that all
my life, not conscious of any of that, I have been
drawn to and instinctively found things “wabi sabi”
appealing. I’ve loved my little hand-carved ivory
Oriental gymnasts for as long as I can remember.
The symmetrical, and expertly hand-woven, earthy
First Nation baskets that my grandmother traded
with her fine silk embroidery, are very special. The
(Continued from page 4)
(Continued on page 6)

September 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page
6
aforementioned steamer trunk always seems to
offer up another new little surprise whenever I look
closely. I built and live in a log house: There is a
never-ending story told by the bug tracks, corked
boot marks, huge randomly shaped logs tightly
fitted to other huge randomly shaped logs, the
startling cracks and snaps late at night (even after
almost fifty years) and the cat face (large scar) intentionally placed in the front wall for all to see as
they approach. The fact that it is the only log house
alongside square and true framed houses speaks to
both my wife’s and my individuality.
So now you know everything about wabi sabi. And
hardly anything at all about wabi sabi. What I feel
is important is to understand that a piece does not
necessarily have to be flawlessly executed in form
and finish to be artistic to convey a story. Just like a
Teddy bear with an eye missing, something can be
appealing and perhaps tell a greater story if it is
imperfect or incomplete. Like a half blind Teddy
bear, that piece can often be closer to you than
you can adequately express.

This Month’s Cover
By Don Gamble
Inspired by the hollow vessels of Mark Gardner,
the initial form was turned during a class with Mark
and later became my canvas for experimentation
with textures and colour. The textured surface
treatment draws loosely from an Art Liestman teapot—specifically one with a fire and rust inspired
patina.
Smooth, untextured areas form my abstracted interpretation of an Aztec mask. Behind this mask,
rage simmers—something volatile, barely restrained, its presence trapped just beneath the surface in ember tones and oxidized textures.
6" tall × 3.5" diameter
Ed. Note: See Don’s more details article about this
project elsewhere in the newsletter

Making A Funeral Urn
By Larry Stevenson
I think that is worthy to go back in time and ask the
question, “Why would I decide to make a funeral
urn?”
I have two daughters that wanted very dearly to
have a family pet and we decided and bought a
Miniature Schnauzer, Molly. She was a wonderful
pet and as time passed she obviously aged and later in life developed grand mal seizures. A very sad
and troubling time for the family and, without any
realistic way of alleviating her condition, it became
obvious that she be put down. It was a very sad
time but what made it harder was when she was
euthanized I was given the choice of having her
cremated or having her remains sent to the dump.
She was my pal, and I obviously chose to have her
cremated. When the task was completed I was notified to come to the vet to pick up her ashes and
she was inside a very
hideous ceramic urn that
didn’t win any accolades
from me. I decided to
make her an urn that I
felt suited her personality. I went to supplier in
Chilliwack and bought a
piece of amboyna burl
and made her an urn
that I felt reflected her
character and the love
she brought to our family. I had to learn to do
hand chased threading but I enjoyed the project.
Friends viewed this urn and I started getting inquiries about whether or not I would consider making
them an urn, some for pets, others for cherished
family members. That is how it all started.
An urn is basically a hollow form with some modifications to it and I am not going to spend a lot of
time describing how to turn a hollow form but will
discuss considerations when making this hollow
form.
First and foremost is the orientation that I use
when making these urns. I always want to do it as
a spindle turning because this orientation leads to
the most stable turning with regards to distortion
of the hole leading into the vessel. I always try and
get the wood wet and rough turn them and dry
them for a very long time allowing the vessel to be
very dry and all distortion or warping has taken
place. Even if I start with supposed dry wood I always leave time to pass to allow warpage. Another
advantage of this orientation is that the figure in
the wood is more prominent, you aren’t looking at
face grain then end grain as you look around the
circumference of the urn.
When you look at this next picture you will see the
small recess that I turn into the end of the vessel.
This allows you to turn a female threaded insert
(Continued on page 8)
Hideous ceramic urn
Small recess in end of vessel

September 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page
8
and have a shoulder to install it against that insures
that it is glued in square to the urn. If you look
closely you may also notice that the top face of the
urn is sloped inwards. This is so that when the lid
is tightened on there is no gap between the urn
body and the lid. Likewise the lid is turned with a
slight inward slope to eliminate this potential problem as well.
Let’s look at all the components that go into making the threaded lid. Originally I turned the lid less
the finial as one piece but this method has a few
setbacks. The most obvious is that when threading
the male portion of the thread you have to be very
quick to pull the thread chaser away from your
work or you will run into the bottom of the lid and
possibly ruin the threads. Secondly, if you mess up
the threads you may also lose the lid portion. I
tend to use African Blackwood for my lids, threads
and finials so given it expense I also don’t want to
mess them up. I have also used Cocobolo for lids
and although this is still relatively expensive, it is
more accessible.
When doing thread chasing you want to use a
wood that is suitable that will thread relatively easily and the denser hardwoods that are sort of waxy
seem to work well. I have used African Blackwood,
Cocobolo and Boxwood and have found that Vine
Maple that has tight growth rings work acceptable
as well. I have had success with Laburnum and also
Black Locust. Try various woods and see what
works for you. It should be a wood with a tight
grain pattern and should be heartwood. It should
also be turned as spindle orientation. If the wood
is marginal, you could try applying a little bit of CA
thin glue onto the threads that you have started.
Many times I simple apply some wax onto the
threads to lubricate them as I am cutting threads.
Learning to chase threads can be frustrating and
for that I have a couple of suggestions.
1. Start by learning to cut threads on a piece of
1.5” or 2” ABS plumbing pipe. Yes, the black
stuff that is used for drains in house construction. Just cut a length of 4 – 6” and put it into
your chuck and square it up and you may also
need to true it up a bit as it can sometimes be
slightly oval. It is cheap and very forgiving.
Once you have learned to cut both male and
female threads on this pipe then move onto
wood.
2. Make yourself a little platform out of a small
length of round stock that fits into your
toolrest. This will ensure that when you are
chasing the female thread, you are holding the
tool level and won’t be at an angle to the desired cut.
Looking back at all the urns I have made I would
have to say that the biggest problem I ran into was
turning the hole for the female thread with the
walls being exactly parallel. Sounds stupid, I know,
but when you are working with small pieces and
they are black it is not easy to see and to ensure
that the walls are parallel. First of all, have a small
LED bright flashlight handy and secondly, I taper
the face to the insert slightly in to ensure that all
pieces mate without any gaps showing. Therefore
(Continued from page 7)
(Continued on page 9)
Lid
Toolrest platform

September 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page
9
you can’t use a traditional square off of the shoulder of the insert to ensure that the sides are parallel. You may think that you could use inside calipers or use the inside arms of Vernier calipers to
ensure parallel sides. I have done that and it is
very difficult due to the dark wood and the small
size. I did find a solution though and I wish I had
have found it years earlier. Lee Valley sells a tool
called a “Cast Masons’ and Engravers’ Square” and
although a simple device it is absolutely changed
my way of dealing with this issue. I have gone back
and looked at some of my older urns and used this
device to check the female threads and some of
them aren’t as good as they could have been. It
has a cast base and uses a small 6” Engineers Rule
as the arm. If you want you could make your own
but this device is now one of my prized possessions.
If you look at the male
threads you will notice
it is on a separate piece.
This is for a good reason. It allows me the
advantage or chasing
the thread without the
worry of bashing into
the lid and also I can select a piece of appropriately sized wood without
wasting extra when turning down to the correct
diameter that I require. African Blackwood isn’t
cheap and I do not want to waste anything. I turn
it with a 1” tenon that then gets glued into the lid.
I guess the obvious next question is how much bigger is the diameter or the male thread blank to the
hole for the female thread insert. Bigger, and although that is a very vague answer it is correct. Bigger!! Too many variables to consider. What is the
thread pitch? (TPI) This affects how deep the
thread is cut. Obviously a thread pitch of 10 TPI
has deeper threads that one of 20 TPI. What I do is
look at my thread chaser and measure the depth of
the thread in it and make the male tenon at least
that much larger that the hole in the female insert.
To top it off I do that after I have ensured that I
have chased the female thread and that I am happy
with it. While I was learning to do thread chasing I
watched many videos from reputable turners and
noticed that the female insert didn’t necessarily
have lots of threads. It definitely makes matching
the pair easier since then the female inserts only
have about 3 threads. Once I have the female insert completed I measure the inside diameter using
a digital caliper and add the thread depth plus a bit
and then turn the blank for the male thread. As I
am chasing the male thread I am constantly stopping and checking the fit against the female insert.
I do apply a bee’s wax onto the male threads as I
am lightly finishing them up to ensure that I have a
nice clean thread. Take your time and try to relax.
It is no fun if you are so uptight that you forget to
breathe.
I should point out here that all the gluing that I am
doing uses an epoxy glue. I use System 3 G2 two
part epoxy glue and I will tell you now that I would
never use a 5 minute epoxy on anything. I have
witnessed many failures with 5 minute epoxy and
given the amount of time I put into my pieces
waiting for glue to cure isn’t an issue. In one of the
evening online discussions we had we discussed
the topic of ensuring that you mix to proper proportions of glue by using a digital scale. I believe it
was a topic that Fraser brought up. Digital scales
are not very expensive and I believe this is an important step to ensure that the glue sets correctly.
The lid has a 1” diameter hole drilled into it and I
do all my final shaping of the lid by using a jam
chuck and first ensuring a tight fit on the waste
(Continued from page 8)
(Continued on page 10)
Cast Masons’ and Engravers’ Square
Separate male threads

September 2025
Greater Vancouver Woodturner's Guild
Page
10
block and then once I am pleased with the shape I
drill a ¼” hole through the lid all the way into the
1” mortise coming from the bottom surface. I also
turn a small 45° bevel on the lid at the top of the
¼” hole. I then do all my sanding at this point. I
sand down to 1 or 2 micron and polish the piece
with Renaissance Wax. As mentioned previously
the lid has the bottom surface sloping inward
slightly.
As with the other pieces I used small blanks that
are used for pens to make the finials. You can use
the small jaws that Oneway manufactures however
I found that the Nova Pen Plus Jaws (SKU 6034)
work wonderfully. There are only two jaws and
they tighten diagonally on the piece so if it isn’t
exactly square there isn’t a problem. You can get
several finials out of one blank. I have found that
to enable myself to get 3 finials out of the one
blank I turn the bottom of the third finial (with the
¼” tenon) while it is secured in the jaws then take
it out. I have made a small piece that has a ¼” mortise with a saw cut into it. I insert the tenon into
this piece and then clamp that into the jaws and
turn the rest of the finial. I have made a story stick
to ensure that the finial that I am turning comes
out as I want it to. At the interface of the finial and
the lid, the finial is also undercut to ensure that it
sits on the lid with no gap.
I do ensure that the finial, the lid and the male
thread piece are all oriented to that the grain lines
up. Why? Maybe because I am fussy but I think it
also provides the illusion that it is all made from
one piece. I am trying to make quality pieces that
will honor the person or creature that ends up inside them and I do believe that caring about how
we construct a piece is important.
The finishing of my urns are by using a spray finish.
I currently use Emtech Water Borne Lacquer (satin)
from Lee Valley. I first apply a coat or two of
Emtech Water Borne Lacquer Sanding Sealer. I also
ensure that the inside is sealed with an acrylic
paint. Various products out there and I don’t have
a preference other that I use black and I highly recommend that you finish the inside to provide a
properly finished urn. You do not want any degradation of the external finish due to the inside not
being sealed.
One of the most asked questions I get is “How big
does an urn have to be?” Very important question
and my answer is big enough that it holds all the
ashes. The general rule is 1 cu.in. for every pound
of weight of the recipient. However, we must consider if the recipient was overweight as during cremation, the excess fat is burned off. Gross sounding, but true. Now you have completed your urn
and you need to determine its volume. How does
one measure such an odd shape? I do it this way. I
fill the finished urn with a sand blasting medium
and measure the weight of this medium on a digital
scale. I then determine the mass of the medium in
a 1 cup measure. Be careful though, not all 1 cup
measures are one cup. You may want to measure
1 cup of water and determine if it is indeed 8 ounces. Once you have an accurate measure of an accurate cup of whatever medium you are using with
some elementary math you can then determine
how may cups it is. Then go on Google and find
out how may cu.in. are in a cup. More math and
you then come up with how many cu.in. the volume of your urn is. You may not have any sandblasting medium to use as a measuring medium, so
what should you use. You could use rice
(preferably uncooked) or some small grain that
doesn’t leave much air space between each piece,
This is why I choose sandblasting medium. Once
you think that urn is full, shake it around to ensure
it settles and add some more if needed. I stop filling when the medium is about ½” below where to
bottom of the lid will be. Of course someone is going to say, why aren’t you determining this in metric measure. I generally do both ways but I’m
getting long in the tooth and still think in imperial
measure.
Take your time and have the urn you make be
something that makes you be proud of the work
that you are able to create.
(Continued from page 9)

Contained Rage: A Turning Journey
By Don Gamble
Over the past several months, I’ve been working on
a hollow form that began during a class with Mark
Gardner. His approach to vessel-making inspired
the initial shape, which later became my canvas for
experimentation
with
texture
and
colour.
When I started, this was never meant to be a finished piece. It began as a practice form—just
something to turn and explore. But as I worked, my
skills evolved. Each decision, each mark, became a stepping stone
in learning how texture
and
colour
interact,
how emotion can be
embedded in surface.
What started as an exercise
gradually
revealed its own voice.
The texturing journey started simply: I wanted to
hide the seam at the midpoint of the form. That
practical decision led to a series of flowing, overlapping
doodles—
organic lines that began
to take on a life of their
own. I textured these
using a micromotor and
a fine Saburrtooth burr,
carving into the surface
with increasing intention. Later, I emphasized
the patterns by using pyrography to burn lines
along the edges to contain the texture, giving it
structure and visual tension.
The surface treatment
colouring draws loosely
from an Art Liestman
teapot—specifically
one with a fire- and
rust-inspired patina. I
used layered acrylics to
build up depth and variation, working in warm
tones that suggest heat
and oxidation. The colour was applied directly to the textured surface, allowing the raised and recessed areas to interact naturally with the paint. This approach
helped reinforce the emotional tone of the piece—
suggesting something smoldering, volatile, and
barely
contained.
Smooth, untextured areas form my abstracted interpretation of an Aztec mask. Behind this mask,
rage simmers—something volatile, barely restrained, its presence trapped just beneath the surface in ember tones and oxidized textures.
The piece is now complete and posted on my Facebook page. Does it evoke the feeling of rage contained behind an Aztec mask? I’d love to hear what
it stirs in you—interpretations, reactions, or suggestions are all welcome.

Operation Rainbow Canada (ORC), is a 100% volunteer, non-profit medical services organization
that in the past has provided free reconstructive
surgery and related health care for cleft lip and
palate deformities, for children in developing
countries. Next year ORC is going to expand their
mandate and treat post burn contractures and
hand deformities as well as cleft lip and palate deformities for both children and adults.
Without ORC, these life altering procedures would
not be possible.
In February 2025 the GVWG volunteered to provide spinning tops to young patients in future
ORC missions in order to ease their anxiety before and after surgery. With the changes to
ORC’s mandate, it would be wonderful if the
Guild could provide spinning tops to not only the
children facing surgery, but to adults facing surgery as well. In cases where hand surgery is
done, the tops might also provide some therapeutic benefit.
ORC has now announced their planned medical
missions for 2026. The first mission will be in
January to Kampala, Uganda. The second mission is tentatively planned for November to India. It is anticipated that approximately 40 patients will be scheduled for surgery for each mission.
Often when families bring their child for surgery,
their siblings travel with them. It would be nice to
be able to have enough spinning tops available so
that the siblings could receive a top as well as the
patients. Let’s see if as a group we can collectively
turn 150 tops for the medical team to take to
Kampala.
Guild members are encouraged to turn and contribute spinning tops for this good cause. Don’t
worry about turning too many tops. They are fun
to turn and if we have too many they can always
be saved and supplied for the second mission in
November.
If you are unsure of how to turn spinning tops,
Matt Lo’s article “Spinning Tops - The Basics” in the
GVWG’s May 2025 Newsletter is an excellent resource.
When turning your tops, please use permanent
colour felt tip markers to make the tops as vibrant
and colourful as possible.
I will collect the tops at the November 27th
meeting. Thanks for your participation.
Guild Challenge - Spinning Tops for Operation Rainbow Canada
By Dex Hallwood

GVWG Group Buy On Sandpaper
By Brian Lunt
Thanks to Bruce Cambell, Alan Jones, and Shirley Watson, our sandpaper
group buy was a success. Delivery took longer than expected as we arranged direct shipping to Canada to avoid USA tariffs. The master rolls
were 100 meters each, so Steve Hansen’s previous 50mt rolling dispenser only partially fit. It still was cool to use.
This guild thrives thanks to many dedicated volunteers.

Lathe Safety: A Hard Lesson Learned
By Brian Lunt
At our guild, safety always comes first in everything
we do in woodturning. We emphasize a wide range
of precautions, from proper lighting and avoiding
tripping hazards with mats, to securing loose clothing and tying back long hair. We pay close attention
to spindle height, tool rest positions, eye and ear
protection, turning speeds, and careful use of band
saws, chainsaws, and grinders. We also check for
hidden cracks in bowl blanks, use the tailstock
whenever possible, hand-turn pieces to check
clearance before starting the lathe, start slowly,
and, importantly, avoid wearing full-fingered
gloves when operating the lathe.
One day, while helping with our group-buy sandpaper project, I made a critical mistake. Instead of
turning wood, we were rolling up multiple grits of
sandpaper as part of this bulk purchase. I wore a
full glove on my dominant right hand, hoping to
protect my fingerprints from being ground down
during the repetitive task. Everything was running
at a slow speed, but in just a tenth of a second of
inattention, the powerful 220v 2 HP Oneway lathe
grabbed the tips of my glove. Instantly, my hand
was pulled into the assembly, winding my arm
around it, crushing my ribs, and scratching my
chest. Even though I hit the stop button immediately, the damage was done.
After waiting for 10 hours in the emergency room, I
received 13 stitches and a splint for my fractured
index finger. It has now been four months since the
accident, and I still haven’t turned anything. My
hand remains awkward and weak, making gripping
difficult and forcing me to rethink how I approach
every task in the shop.
My hand is getting better through great physio encouragement ( thanks Wanda ) and lots of specific
exercises and time.
The lesson here is clear: never use full gloves at the
lathe. Full gloves can easily get caught in spinning
machinery, pulling your hands into dangerous positions before you have a chance to react. Instead,
opt for open-finger gloves when rough turning bark
-covered blanks, or avoid gloves entirely when
working near moving parts. Taking this extra precaution can prevent painful injuries and long recoveries.
Sharing my experience has changed how I think
about safety. I now double-check everything before turning on the lathe, remain hyper-aware of
my surroundings, and want to remind guild members to stay vigilant. I hope my story helps others
avoid similar mistakes and underscores the importance of following every safety recommendation, no matter how minor it may seem.

Safety Guidelines for Woodturning
You mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility
 Always wear safety goggles or safety
glasses that include side protectors.
Use a full face shield for bowl, vessel, or
any turning involving chucks and faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/
or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder and
wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting
wrenches, and knockout bars immediately after use. Never leave them in
place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose
clothing, jewelry, or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating parts
or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the
workpiece is solidly mounted with stout
screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws
as a minimum). Do not use dry wall or
deck screws.
 When turning between centres, be certain the workpiece is firmly mounted
between the headstock driving centre
and tailstock centre.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in
place.
 Check that all locking devices on the
tailstock and tool rest assembly (rest
and base) are tight before operating the
lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by
hand to make sure it clears the toolrest
and bed before turning the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind
and in front of the workpiece, they are
the most likely areas for a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of this zone when
turning on the lathe, keeping your hand
on the switch in case you need to turn
the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning it on. Use slower speeds
for larger diameters or rough pieces
and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the
lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always
stop the machine to verify why. As a
starting point, consult your operator’s
manual for recommended speeds for a
particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed
is compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock

28
with cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets,
knots, irregular shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid these types
of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the
toolrest, holding the tool in a controlled
but comfortable manner. Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless it is securely
tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations.
An experienced woodturner is capable
of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning
turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before
sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing,
and keep your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check
for damaged parts, alignment, binding
of moving parts, and other conditions
that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better
and safer performance. Don’t force a
dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose
for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t
use a lathe in damp or wet locations.
Do not use in presence of flammable
liquids or gases, and always keep a fully
-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing.
Pay close attention to unusual sounds
or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate machines
when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect
electric cords for damage. Avoid the
use of extension cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn power off. Don’t leave
lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially band and
chain saws. Learn and follow the safety
guidelines for this equipment.
For more information on woodturning
safety please visit the AAW’s Woodturning Safety webpage and GVWG Safety
webpage.
